lead: A regular expression is a finite formula that describes a language. Its atoms are the empty set ∅, the empty string ε, and each symbol a of an alphabet Σ. Union, concatenation and Kleene star combine atoms into bigger expressions. Precedence removes most brackets: star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union. A search box, a grep command or an input validator often uses this same notation, because a short pattern must accept exactly the strings that match and reject the rest.
prereq: You need Unit 1 on alphabets, strings and languages, especially Σ*, concatenation and Kleene star, and the language operations in alphabets and strings.

sections.h3: Atoms, operators and the language denoted

blocks.text: Fix a finite alphabet Σ. A string is a finite sequence of symbols from Σ. Σ* is the set of all such strings, including ε. A language is any subset of Σ*. A regular expression over Σ is a finite formula built by the rules below.

items: Base rule 1: ∅ is a regular expression and denotes the empty language ∅.
Base rule 2: ε is a regular expression and denotes {ε}.
Base rule 3: each a ∈ Σ is a regular expression and denotes {a}.
Inductive rule: if r and s are regular expressions, then (r+s), (rs) and (r*) are regular expressions.

blocks.text: Some books write r|s instead of r+s. Concatenation is written by juxtaposition: rs means r followed by s. A centred dot is not standard for concatenation here; it is used only when explaining a parse.

blocks.where: r and s are regular expressions; L(r) is the language denoted by r; + is union, also written | in some books.
L(r)L(s) is the concatenation of the two languages: every string xy with x in L(r) and y in L(s).

blocks.text: L(r*) = {w1w2...wk | k ≥ 0 and each wi ∈ L(r)}
blocks.where: k is the number of repetitions; k = 0 gives ε, so ε is always in L(r*). The set L(r) is also called a regular set.

blocks.text: Over Σ = {0,1}: 0 denotes {0}; ε denotes {ε}; ∅ denotes ∅; 0+1 denotes {0,1}; 01 denotes {01}; 0* denotes {ε,0,00,...}; (0+1)* denotes all binary strings.

sections.h3: Precedence: star, then concatenation, then union

blocks.text: Precedence fixes the order of operations when brackets are omitted. Highest is Kleene star. Next is concatenation. Lowest is union. Operators of equal precedence group from left to right.

items: First attach each star to the smallest preceding expression: a single symbol, a bracketed group, or an already starred expression.
Second group concatenations from left to right.
Third group unions from left to right.

blocks.text: Example: 0+1(01)*. The brackets (01) are concatenation 0·1. The star applies to that whole group, giving (0·1)*. Concatenation joins 1 to that star, giving 1·(0·1)*. Union is last, so the full expression is 0 ∪ (1·(0·1)*). The left 0 is not starred, and the star does not apply to the leading 1.

Some syllabi write union as |. Thus a+b and a|b denote the same language. Spaces and line breaks change nothing. Parentheses can always be added for clarity, even where precedence would allow omission. A pair of parentheses around a whole expression, such as (0+1), is allowed but not needed.

To build an expression from a short description, name the pieces and put the weakest operator at the top. For 'a 0 followed by any number of 01 pairs', write 0(01)*. For 'either a single 0 or a 1 followed by any number of 01 pairs', write 0+1(01)*. For 'any string of 0s and 1s that ends in 1', write (0+1)*1.

To check an expression, compute its language from the inside out. List the atoms. Apply stars to the smallest possible groups. Concatenate adjacent languages by writing every pair xy with x from the left language and y from the right language. Union takes all strings from both languages. To test short strings by hand, generate strings by length from 0 upward and check membership.

Two atoms look alike but are different. ∅ is a language with no strings. ε is a language with one string of length 0. Therefore ∅* = {ε} and ε* = {ε}. Also ∅+ε denotes {ε}, not ∅. Star on ∅ never creates 0 or 1. Simplifying an expression uses the laws in Chapter 2.2; turning it into a machine is Chapter 2.3.

examples.question: Over Σ = {0,1}, use precedence to parenthesise 0 + 1(01)* and list every string of length at most 3 in its language.
steps: Alphabet: Σ = {0,1}. The atoms are 0, 1, 0 and 1.
Star next: (01)* = (0·1)*. It repeats the two-symbol block 01.
Concatenation next: 1(01)* = 1·(0·1)*. The leading 1 is outside the star.

List by length. Length 0: no string, because neither part gives ε. Length 1: 0 from the left; 1 from the right with zero repetitions. Length 2: 0 ∪ 1(01)* contains no length-2 string. Length 3: 101 from 1 followed by one copy of 01. The next string from the right is 10101, length 5, so it is excluded.
The strings of length at most 3 are 0, 1 and 101.
examples.answer: The fully parenthesised expression is 0 ∪ (1·(0·1)*), and its strings of length at most 3 are 0, 1 and 101; there are 3 such strings.

traps: ∅ is not ε. L(∅)=∅ has no strings; L(ε)={ε} has one string of length 0. So ∅*={ε}.
Concatenation is juxtaposition, not a centred dot: write 01, not 0·1, unless you are explaining the parse.
Star binds tighter than union: 0+1* means 0 ∪ (1*), not (0+1)*.
Parentheses override precedence: (01)* is not 01*. The first repeats 01; the second is a 0 followed by any number of 1s.
Union is sometimes written + and sometimes |; do not mix them in one expression unless the notation is defined.

quiz.q: List the three atomic kinds of regular expression over an alphabet Σ and the language each denotes.
quiz.a: ∅ denotes the empty language ∅; ε denotes {ε}; each a ∈ Σ denotes {a}.

quiz.q: State the precedence order of star, concatenation and union.
quiz.a: Highest is star, then concatenation, lowest is union.

quiz.q: Explain why ∅ and ε are not the same regular expression.
quiz.a: L(∅) is the empty set, with no strings. L(ε) is {ε}, one string of length 0. Thus ∅*={ε}, while ε*={ε} also, but ∅ and ε themselves differ.

quiz.q: Fully parenthesise a+bc* using ∪ for union and · for concatenation.
quiz.a: Star first: c*. Concatenation next: b·(c*). Union last: a ∪ (b·(c*)).

quiz.q: Over Σ = {0,1}, list all strings of length at most 2 in L(0+1*).
quiz.a: L(1*) has ε, 1 and 11 up to length 2. Adding 0 gives ε, 0, 1 and 11. The string 0 has length 1; ε has length 0.

quiz.q: Show that concatenation is not commutative by giving two expressions r and s over {a,b} with L(rs) ≠ L(sr).
quiz.a: Take r=a and s=b. L(ab)={ab}, while L(ba)={ba}. These languages differ, so order matters.

quiz.q: A student reads 01* as (01)*. Give one string accepted by 01* but not by (01)*.
quiz.a: The string 0 is in 01* because the star allows zero 1s, giving 0. But 0 is not in (01)*, which contains only ε, 01, 0101, and so on.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real programming-language regex engines add backreferences, lookahead and greedy matching; these can recognise some non-regular languages, so they are not the regular expressions of this unit. Search for Thompson's construction, RE2, and regular-expression derivatives to see how libraries compile patterns into automata. The same theory underlies lexers, log filters and DNA pattern search. Regex denial of service is a practical warning that a badly written pattern can backtrack for a long time.
